vignette: Diego Hernandez still remembers the sound of crunching metal and screams that filled the air on that fateful day when a car crashed into the bus he was riding home from work. The accident left him shaken, but what's been even more disturbing is the way his mind keeps replaying the scene, wondering if there was anything he could have done to prevent it. Whenever discussions about accidents or crashes come up, Diego feels himself becoming detached, as if observing the conversation from outside his body. He tries to shake off the feeling, telling himself it's just a normal response, but deep down, he knows it's not. These conversations trigger a cascade of thoughts about how life would have been different if the accident hadn't occurred - what job he'd be working at, who he'd be dating, where he'd be living. This counterfactual thinking has become an all-consuming habit, taking up hours of his day as he mentally rewrites history. But it's not just conversations that set him off; media coverage of similar events sends Diego down a rabbit hole of despair. Watching TV programmes or reading about accidents makes him feel like the world is a treacherous place where anything can happen at any moment, and no one is safe. He's started avoiding news and media altogether, afraid of being confronted with the grim reality he's trying to escape. As Diego navigates his days, these triggers keep reinforcing a nagging sense of guilt and responsibility for not protecting others during the accident. "I should have done something," he tells himself repeatedly, replaying the moments leading up to the crash in his mind. This self-blame has morphed into a broader fear that harm can come from anywhere, at any time - a constant threat lurking just beneath the surface. Feeling trapped by these thoughts and memories, Diego has become increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings or events where police might be present. He knows it's irrational, but seeing officers in uniform sends him spiralling back to that terrible day. He's even stopped meeting friends at restaurants near major roads, afraid of being reminded of the accident. Lately, Diego's started to feel like nothing good can happen to him anymore - as if he's cursed to relive this traumatic event forever. This dread colours every waking moment, from his daily commute to work as a QA engineer to his quiet nights spent alone at home. It's gotten so bad that even small pleasures like watching sports or listening to music feel tainted by the crushing weight of his negative thoughts. As Diego struggles to keep these emotions in check, he finds himself trapped in a cycle of avoidance and counterfactual thinking. He knows it's not healthy, but it feels safer than confronting the raw emotions beneath - emotions that seem to be growing more intense with each passing day. It's this increasing desperation, coupled with his worsening isolation, that has finally driven Diego to seek help - hoping to find a way out of this suffocating cycle and into a future where he can learn to live with himself again.
